To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) wrist-worn motion sensor alone cannot recognize all activities; (2) the combination of wrist-worn and mobile phone motion sensor improves the activity recognition accuracy, especially at smaller segmentation windows; and (3) larger window sizes are more appropriate for less repetitive activities, like smoking, eating, talking and drinking coffee.

(a) wrist position outperforms pocket position, (b) the combination of wrist and pocket positions outperforms wrist position alone, and (c) the combination of the three motion sensors at both wrist and trouser pocket positions is more effective than using only a single sensor.

the combination of the wrist position and the trouser pocket position outperforms the trouser pocket alone, especially at small segmentation windows, and that increasing the segmentation window size improves the recognition of less-repetitive, hand-gesture based activities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the recognition of less-repetitive human activities and we show the importance of using multiple sensor positions and window sizes.
two problems in human activity recognition: 1) how to combine the information from two positions and 2) the impact of window size on the recognition of various activities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
wrist-worn and pocket-worn sensors are complementary and that the use of both sensors improves activity recognition.
wrist and pocket positions can be used in conjunction for better activity recognition.
wrist and trouser pocket motion sensors should be used together to recognize human activities and that the choice of the window size is an important factor to consider.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we propose a novel way of combining on-body motion sensors at the wrist and pocket positions, evaluate the effect of window size on various activities and propose optimizations to improve the recognition of less-repetitive and less-discriminatory activities.
the combination of wrist-worn and smartphone motion sensors can recognize a variety of human activities, including less-repetitive ones, at various segmentation windows.

the combination of wrist and pocket positions outperform the use of wrist position alone, but the use of larger segmentation window sizes improves the recognition of less-repetitive and less-frequent activities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
using two positions (pocket and wrist) together can improve the recognition of complex activities.
wrist-worn motion sensing is more effective than on-body sensing for recognizing less-repetitive human activities.

the wrist position is better suited for recognizing less repetitive activities, such as giving a talk, smoking and eating, while the pocket position is better suited to recognizing more repetitive activities, such a walking, jogging, and biking.
